Transformers-based Encoder-Decoder Models

Published October 10, 2020

This article is also available in Chinese 简体中文 .

!pip install transformers==4.2.1 !pip install sentencepiece==0.1.95

The transformer-based encoder-decoder model was introduced by Vaswani et al. in the famous Attention is all you need paper and is today the de-facto standard encoder-decoder architecture in natural language processing (NLP).

Recently, there has been a lot of research on different pre-training objectives for transformer-based encoder-decoder models, e.g. T5, Bart, Pegasus, ProphetNet, Marge, etc ..., but the model architecture has stayed largely the same.

The goal of the blog post is to give an in-detail explanation of how the transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture models sequence-to-sequence problems. We will focus on the mathematical model defined by the architecture and how the model can be used in inference. Along the way, we will give some background on sequence-to-sequence models in NLP and break down the transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture into its encoder and decoder parts. We provide many illustrations and establish the link between the theory of transformer-based encoder-decoder models and their practical usage in 🤗Transformers for inference. Note that this blog post does not explain how such models can be trained - this will be the topic of a future blog post.

Transformer-based encoder-decoder models are the result of years of research on representation learning and model architectures . This notebook provides a short summary of the history of neural encoder-decoder models. For more context, the reader is advised to read this awesome blog post by Sebastion Ruder. Additionally, a basic understanding of the self-attention architecture is recommended. The following blog post by Jay Alammar serves as a good refresher on the original Transformer model here .

At the time of writing this notebook, 🤗Transformers comprises the encoder-decoder models T5 , Bart , MarianMT , and Pegasus , which are summarized in the docs under model summaries .

The notebook is divided into four parts:

Background - A short history of neural encoder-decoder models is given with a focus on RNN-based models.

Encoder-Decoder - The transformer-based encoder-decoder model is presented and it is explained how the model is used for inference.

Encoder - The encoder part of the model is explained in detail.

Decoder - The decoder part of the model is explained in detail.

Each part builds upon the previous part, but can also be read on its own.

Tasks in natural language generation (NLG), a subfield of NLP, are best expressed as sequence-to-sequence problems. Such tasks can be defined as finding a model that maps a sequence of input words to a sequence of target words. Some classic examples are summarization and translation . In the following, we assume that each word is encoded into a vector representation. n n n input words can then be represented as a sequence of n n n input vectors:

X 1 : n = { x 1 , … , x n } . \mathbf{X}_{1:n} = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n\}. X 1 : n ​ = { x 1 ​ , … , x n ​ } .

Consequently, sequence-to-sequence problems can be solved by finding a mapping f f f from an input sequence of n n n vectors X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ to a sequence of m m m target vectors Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ , whereas the number of target vectors m m m is unknown apriori and depends on the input sequence:

f : X 1 : n → Y 1 : m . f: \mathbf{X}_{1:n} \to \mathbf{Y}_{1:m}. f : X 1 : n ​ → Y 1 : m ​ .

Sutskever et al. (2014) noted that deep neural networks (DNN)s, "*despite their flexibility and power can only define a mapping whose inputs and targets can be sensibly encoded with vectors of fixed dimensionality.*" 1 {}^1 1

Using a DNN model 2 {}^2 2 to solve sequence-to-sequence problems would therefore mean that the number of target vectors m m m has to be known apriori and would have to be independent of the input X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ . This is suboptimal because, for tasks in NLG, the number of target words usually depends on the input X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ and not just on the input length n n n . E.g. , an article of 1000 words can be summarized to both 200 words and 100 words depending on its content.

In 2014, Cho et al. and Sutskever et al. proposed to use an encoder-decoder model purely based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for sequence-to-sequence tasks. In contrast to DNNS, RNNs are capable of modeling a mapping to a variable number of target vectors. Let's dive a bit deeper into the functioning of RNN-based encoder-decoder models.

During inference, the encoder RNN encodes an input sequence X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ by successively updating its hidden state 3 {}^3 3 . After having processed the last input vector x n \mathbf{x}_n x n ​ , the encoder's hidden state defines the input encoding c \mathbf{c} c . Thus, the encoder defines the mapping:

f θ e n c : X 1 : n → c . f_{\theta_{enc}}: \mathbf{X}_{1:n} \to \mathbf{c}. f θ e n c ​ ​ : X 1 : n ​ → c .

Then, the decoder's hidden state is initialized with the input encoding and during inference, the decoder RNN is used to auto-regressively generate the target sequence. Let's explain.

Mathematically, the decoder defines the probability distribution of a target sequence Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ given the hidden state c \mathbf{c} c :

p θ d e c ( Y 1 : m ∣ c ) . p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:m} |\mathbf{c}). p θ d ec ​ ​ ( Y 1 : m ​ ∣ c ) .

By Bayes' rule the distribution can be decomposed into conditional distributions of single target vectors as follows:

p θ d e c ( Y 1 : m ∣ c ) = ∏ i = 1 m p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , c ) . p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:m} |\mathbf{c}) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{c}). p θ d ec ​ ​ ( Y 1 : m ​ ∣ c ) = i = 1 ∏ m ​ p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , c ) .

Thus, if the architecture can model the conditional distribution of the next target vector, given all previous target vectors:

p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , c ) , ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , m } , p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{c}), \forall i \in \{1, \ldots, m\}, p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , c ) , ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , m } ,

then it can model the distribution of any target vector sequence given the hidden state c \mathbf{c} c by simply multiplying all conditional probabilities.

So how does the RNN-based decoder architecture model p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , c ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{c}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , c ) ?

In computational terms, the model sequentially maps the previous inner hidden state c i − 1 \mathbf{c}_{i-1} c i − 1 ​ and the previous target vector y i − 1 \mathbf{y}_{i-1} y i − 1 ​ to the current inner hidden state c i \mathbf{c}_i c i ​ and a logit vector l i \mathbf{l}_i l i ​ (shown in dark red below):

f θ dec ( y i − 1 , c i − 1 ) → l i , c i . f_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_{i-1}, \mathbf{c}_{i-1}) \to \mathbf{l}_i, \mathbf{c}_i. f θ dec ​ ​ ( y i − 1 ​ , c i − 1 ​ ) → l i ​ , c i ​ . c 0 \mathbf{c}_0 c 0 ​ is thereby defined as c \mathbf{c} c being the output hidden state of the RNN-based encoder. Subsequently, the softmax operation is used to transform the logit vector l i \mathbf{l}_i l i ​ to a conditional probablity distribution of the next target vector:

p ( y i ∣ l i ) = Softmax ( l i ) , with l i = f θ dec ( y i − 1 , c prev ) . p(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{l}_i) = \textbf{Softmax}(\mathbf{l}_i), \text{ with } \mathbf{l}_i = f_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_{i-1}, \mathbf{c}_{\text{prev}}). p ( y i ​ ∣ l i ​ ) = Softmax ( l i ​ ) , with l i ​ = f θ dec ​ ​ ( y i − 1 ​ , c prev ​ ) .

For more detail on the logit vector and the resulting probability distribution, please see footnote 4 {}^4 4 . From the above equation, we can see that the distribution of the current target vector y i \mathbf{y}_i y i ​ is directly conditioned on the previous target vector y i − 1 \mathbf{y}_{i-1} y i − 1 ​ and the previous hidden state c i − 1 \mathbf{c}_{i-1} c i − 1 ​ . Because the previous hidden state c i − 1 \mathbf{c}_{i-1} c i − 1 ​ depends on all previous target vectors y 0 , … , y i − 2 \mathbf{y}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{y}_{i-2} y 0 ​ , … , y i − 2 ​ , it can be stated that the RNN-based decoder implicitly ( e.g. indirectly ) models the conditional distribution p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , c ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{c}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , c ) .

The space of possible target vector sequences Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ is prohibitively large so that at inference, one has to rely on decoding methods 5 {}^5 5 that efficiently sample high probability target vector sequences from p θ d e c ( Y 1 : m ∣ c ) p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:m} |\mathbf{c}) p θ d ec ​ ​ ( Y 1 : m ​ ∣ c ) .

Given such a decoding method, during inference, the next input vector y i \mathbf{y}_i y i ​ can then be sampled from p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , c ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{c}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , c ) and is consequently appended to the input sequence so that the decoder RNN then models p θ dec ( y i + 1 ∣ Y 0 : i , c ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_{i+1} | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i}, \mathbf{c}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i + 1 ​ ∣ Y 0 : i ​ , c ) to sample the next input vector y i + 1 \mathbf{y}_{i+1} y i + 1 ​ and so on in an auto-regressive fashion.

An important feature of RNN-based encoder-decoder models is the definition of special vectors, such as the EOS \text{EOS} EOS and BOS \text{BOS} BOS vector. The EOS \text{EOS} EOS vector often represents the final input vector x n \mathbf{x}_n x n ​ to "cue" the encoder that the input sequence has ended and also defines the end of the target sequence. As soon as the EOS \text{EOS} EOS is sampled from a logit vector, the generation is complete. The BOS \text{BOS} BOS vector represents the input vector y 0 \mathbf{y}_0 y 0 ​ fed to the decoder RNN at the very first decoding step. To output the first logit l 1 \mathbf{l}_1 l 1 ​ , an input is required and since no input has been generated at the first step a special BOS \text{BOS} BOS input vector is fed to the decoder RNN. Ok - quite complicated! Let's illustrate and walk through an example.

The unfolded RNN encoder is colored in green and the unfolded RNN decoder is colored in red.

The English sentence "I want to buy a car", represented by x 1 = I \mathbf{x}_1 = \text{I} x 1 ​ = I , x 2 = want \mathbf{x}_2 = \text{want} x 2 ​ = want , x 3 = to \mathbf{x}_3 = \text{to} x 3 ​ = to , x 4 = buy \mathbf{x}_4 = \text{buy} x 4 ​ = buy , x 5 = a \mathbf{x}_5 = \text{a} x 5 ​ = a , x 6 = car \mathbf{x}_6 = \text{car} x 6 ​ = car and x 7 = EOS \mathbf{x}_7 = \text{EOS} x 7 ​ = EOS is translated into German: "Ich will ein Auto kaufen" defined as y 0 = BOS \mathbf{y}_0 = \text{BOS} y 0 ​ = BOS , y 1 = Ich \mathbf{y}_1 = \text{Ich} y 1 ​ = Ich , y 2 = will \mathbf{y}_2 = \text{will} y 2 ​ = will , y 3 = ein \mathbf{y}_3 = \text{ein} y 3 ​ = ein , y 4 = Auto , y 5 = kaufen \mathbf{y}_4 = \text{Auto}, \mathbf{y}_5 = \text{kaufen} y 4 ​ = Auto , y 5 ​ = kaufen and y 6 = EOS \mathbf{y}_6=\text{EOS} y 6 ​ = EOS . To begin with, the input vector x 1 = I \mathbf{x}_1 = \text{I} x 1 ​ = I is processed by the encoder RNN and updates its hidden state. Note that because we are only interested in the final encoder's hidden state c \mathbf{c} c , we can disregard the RNN encoder's target vector. The encoder RNN then processes the rest of the input sentence want \text{want} want , to \text{to} to , buy \text{buy} buy , a \text{a} a , car \text{car} car , EOS \text{EOS} EOS in the same fashion, updating its hidden state at each step until the vector x 7 = E O S \mathbf{x}_7={EOS} x 7 ​ = EOS is reached 6 {}^6 6 . In the illustration above the horizontal arrow connecting the unfolded encoder RNN represents the sequential updates of the hidden state. The final hidden state of the encoder RNN, represented by c \mathbf{c} c then completely defines the encoding of the input sequence and is used as the initial hidden state of the decoder RNN. This can be seen as conditioning the decoder RNN on the encoded input.

To generate the first target vector, the decoder is fed the BOS \text{BOS} BOS vector, illustrated as y 0 \mathbf{y}_0 y 0 ​ in the design above. The target vector of the RNN is then further mapped to the logit vector l 1 \mathbf{l}_1 l 1 ​ by means of the LM Head feed-forward layer to define the conditional distribution of the first target vector as explained above:

p θ d e c ( y ∣ BOS , c ) . p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{y} | \text{BOS}, \mathbf{c}). p θ d ec ​ ​ ( y ∣ BOS , c ) .

The word Ich \text{Ich} Ich is sampled (shown by the grey arrow, connecting l 1 \mathbf{l}_1 l 1 ​ and y 1 \mathbf{y}_1 y 1 ​ ) and consequently the second target vector can be sampled:

will ∼ p θ d e c ( y ∣ BOS , Ich , c ) . \text{will} \sim p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{y} | \text{BOS}, \text{Ich}, \mathbf{c}). will ∼ p θ d ec ​ ​ ( y ∣ BOS , Ich , c ) .

And so on until at step i = 6 i=6 i = 6 , the EOS \text{EOS} EOS vector is sampled from l 6 \mathbf{l}_6 l 6 ​ and the decoding is finished. The resulting target sequence amounts to Y 1 : 6 = { y 1 , … , y 6 } \mathbf{Y}_{1:6} = \{\mathbf{y}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{y}_6\} Y 1 : 6 ​ = { y 1 ​ , … , y 6 ​ } , which is "Ich will ein Auto kaufen" in our example above.

To sum it up, an RNN-based encoder-decoder model, represented by f θ enc f_{\theta_{\text{enc}}} f θ enc ​ ​ and p θ dec p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}} p θ dec ​ ​ defines the distribution p ( Y 1 : m ∣ X 1 : n ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{1:m} | \mathbf{X}_{1:n}) p ( Y 1 : m ​ ∣ X 1 : n ​ ) by factorization:

p θ enc , θ dec ( Y 1 : m ∣ X 1 : n ) = ∏ i = 1 m p θ enc , θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , X 1 : n ) = ∏ i = 1 m p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , c ) , with c = f θ e n c ( X ) . p_{\theta_{\text{enc}}, \theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:m} | \mathbf{X}_{1:n}) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} p_{\theta_{\text{enc}}, \theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{X}_{1:n}) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{c}), \text{ with } \mathbf{c}=f_{\theta_{enc}}(X). p θ enc ​ , θ dec ​ ​ ( Y 1 : m ​ ∣ X 1 : n ​ ) = i = 1 ∏ m ​ p θ enc ​ , θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , X 1 : n ​ ) = i = 1 ∏ m ​ p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , c ) , with c = f θ e n c ​ ​ ( X ) .

During inference, efficient decoding methods can auto-regressively generate the target sequence Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ .

The RNN-based encoder-decoder model took the NLG community by storm. In 2016, Google announced to fully replace its heavily feature engineered translation service by a single RNN-based encoder-decoder model (see here ).

Nevertheless, RNN-based encoder-decoder models have two pitfalls. First, RNNs suffer from the vanishing gradient problem, making it very difficult to capture long-range dependencies, cf. Hochreiter et al. (2001) . Second, the inherent recurrent architecture of RNNs prevents efficient parallelization when encoding, cf. Vaswani et al. (2017) .

1 {}^1 1 The original quote from the paper is " Despite their flexibility and power, DNNs can only be applied to problems whose inputs and targets can be sensibly encoded with vectors of fixed dimensionality ", which is slightly adapted here.

2 {}^2 2 The same holds essentially true for convolutional neural networks (CNNs). While an input sequence of variable length can be fed into a CNN, the dimensionality of the target will always be dependent on the input dimensionality or fixed to a specific value.

3 {}^3 3 At the first step, the hidden state is initialized as a zero vector and fed to the RNN together with the first input vector x 1 \mathbf{x}_1 x 1 ​ .

4 {}^4 4 A neural network can define a probability distribution over all words, i.e. p ( y ∣ c , Y 0 : i − 1 ) p(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}) p ( y ∣ c , Y 0 : i − 1 ​ ) as follows. First, the network defines a mapping from the inputs c , Y 0 : i − 1 \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1} c , Y 0 : i − 1 ​ to an embedded vector representation y ′ \mathbf{y'} y ′ , which corresponds to the RNN target vector. The embedded vector representation y ′ \mathbf{y'} y ′ is then passed to the "language model head" layer, which means that it is multiplied by the word embedding matrix , i.e. Y vocab \mathbf{Y}^{\text{vocab}} Y vocab , so that a score between y ′ \mathbf{y'} y ′ and each encoded vector y ∈ Y vocab \mathbf{y} \in \mathbf{Y}^{\text{vocab}} y ∈ Y vocab is computed. The resulting vector is called the logit vector l = Y vocab y ′ \mathbf{l} = \mathbf{Y}^{\text{vocab}} \mathbf{y'} l = Y vocab y ′ and can be mapped to a probability distribution over all words by applying a softmax operation: p ( y ∣ c ) = Softmax ( Y vocab y ′ ) = Softmax ( l ) p(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{c}) = \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{Y}^{\text{vocab}} \mathbf{y'}) = \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{l}) p ( y ∣ c ) = Softmax ( Y vocab y ′ ) = Softmax ( l ) .

6 {}^6 6 Sutskever et al. (2014) reverses the order of the input so that in the above example the input vectors would correspond to x 1 = car \mathbf{x}_1 = \text{car} x 1 ​ = car , x 2 = a \mathbf{x}_2 = \text{a} x 2 ​ = a , x 3 = buy \mathbf{x}_3 = \text{buy} x 3 ​ = buy , x 4 = to \mathbf{x}_4 = \text{to} x 4 ​ = to , x 5 = want \mathbf{x}_5 = \text{want} x 5 ​ = want , x 6 = I \mathbf{x}_6 = \text{I} x 6 ​ = I and x 7 = EOS \mathbf{x}_7 = \text{EOS} x 7 ​ = EOS . The motivation is to allow for a shorter connection between corresponding word pairs such as x 6 = I \mathbf{x}_6 = \text{I} x 6 ​ = I and y 1 = Ich \mathbf{y}_1 = \text{Ich} y 1 ​ = Ich . The research group emphasizes that the reversal of the input sequence was a key reason for their model's improved performance on machine translation.

In 2017, Vaswani et al. introduced the Transformer and thereby gave birth to transformer-based encoder-decoder models.

Analogous to RNN-based encoder-decoder models, transformer-based encoder-decoder models consist of an encoder and a decoder which are both stacks of residual attention blocks . The key innovation of transformer-based encoder-decoder models is that such residual attention blocks can process an input sequence X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ of variable length n n n without exhibiting a recurrent structure. Not relying on a recurrent structure allows transformer-based encoder-decoders to be highly parallelizable, which makes the model orders of magnitude more computationally efficient than RNN-based encoder-decoder models on modern hardware.

As a reminder, to solve a sequence-to-sequence problem, we need to find a mapping of an input sequence X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ to an output sequence Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ of variable length m m m . Let's see how transformer-based encoder-decoder models are used to find such a mapping.

Similar to RNN-based encoder-decoder models, the transformer-based encoder-decoder models define a conditional distribution of target vectors Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ given an input sequence X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ :

p θ enc , θ dec ( Y 1 : m ∣ X 1 : n ) . p_{\theta_{\text{enc}}, \theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:m} | \mathbf{X}_{1:n}). p θ enc ​ , θ dec ​ ​ ( Y 1 : m ​ ∣ X 1 : n ​ ) .

The transformer-based encoder part encodes the input sequence X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ to a sequence of hidden states X ‾ 1 : n \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ , thus defining the mapping:

f θ enc : X 1 : n → X ‾ 1 : n . f_{\theta_{\text{enc}}}: \mathbf{X}_{1:n} \to \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}. f θ enc ​ ​ : X 1 : n ​ → X 1 : n ​ .

The transformer-based decoder part then models the conditional probability distribution of the target vector sequence Y 1 : n \mathbf{Y}_{1:n} Y 1 : n ​ given the sequence of encoded hidden states X ‾ 1 : n \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ :

p θ d e c ( Y 1 : n ∣ X ‾ 1 : n ) . p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:n} | \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}). p θ d ec ​ ​ ( Y 1 : n ​ ∣ X 1 : n ​ ) .

By Bayes' rule, this distribution can be factorized to a product of conditional probability distribution of the target vector y i \mathbf{y}_i y i ​ given the encoded hidden states X ‾ 1 : n \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ and all previous target vectors Y 0 : i − 1 \mathbf{Y}_{0:i-1} Y 0 : i − 1 ​ :

p θ d e c ( Y 1 : n ∣ X ‾ 1 : n ) = ∏ i = 1 n p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , X ‾ 1 : n ) . p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:n} | \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}). p θ d ec ​ ​ ( Y 1 : n ​ ∣ X 1 : n ​ ) = i = 1 ∏ n ​ p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , X 1 : n ​ ) .

The transformer-based decoder hereby maps the sequence of encoded hidden states X ‾ 1 : n \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ and all previous target vectors Y 0 : i − 1 \mathbf{Y}_{0:i-1} Y 0 : i − 1 ​ to the logit vector l i \mathbf{l}_i l i ​ . The logit vector l i \mathbf{l}_i l i ​ is then processed by the softmax operation to define the conditional distribution p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , X ‾ 1 : n ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , X 1 : n ​ ) , just as it is done for RNN-based decoders. However, in contrast to RNN-based decoders, the distribution of the target vector y i \mathbf{y}_i y i ​ is explicitly (or directly) conditioned on all previous target vectors y 0 , … , y i − 1 \mathbf{y}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{y}_{i-1} y 0 ​ , … , y i − 1 ​ as we will see later in more detail. The 0th target vector y 0 \mathbf{y}_0 y 0 ​ is hereby represented by a special "begin-of-sentence" BOS \text{BOS} BOS vector.

Having defined the conditional distribution p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , X ‾ 1 : n ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , X 1 : n ​ ) , we can now auto-regressively generate the output and thus define a mapping of an input sequence X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ to an output sequence Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ at inference.

Let's visualize the complete process of auto-regressive generation of transformer-based encoder-decoder models.

The transformer-based encoder is colored in green and the transformer-based decoder is colored in red. As in the previous section, we show how the English sentence "I want to buy a car", represented by x 1 = I \mathbf{x}_1 = \text{I} x 1 ​ = I , x 2 = want \mathbf{x}_2 = \text{want} x 2 ​ = want , x 3 = to \mathbf{x}_3 = \text{to} x 3 ​ = to , x 4 = buy \mathbf{x}_4 = \text{buy} x 4 ​ = buy , x 5 = a \mathbf{x}_5 = \text{a} x 5 ​ = a , x 6 = car \mathbf{x}_6 = \text{car} x 6 ​ = car , and x 7 = EOS \mathbf{x}_7 = \text{EOS} x 7 ​ = EOS is translated into German: "Ich will ein Auto kaufen" defined as y 0 = BOS \mathbf{y}_0 = \text{BOS} y 0 ​ = BOS , y 1 = Ich \mathbf{y}_1 = \text{Ich} y 1 ​ = Ich , y 2 = will \mathbf{y}_2 = \text{will} y 2 ​ = will , y 3 = ein \mathbf{y}_3 = \text{ein} y 3 ​ = ein , y 4 = Auto , y 5 = kaufen \mathbf{y}_4 = \text{Auto}, \mathbf{y}_5 = \text{kaufen} y 4 ​ = Auto , y 5 ​ = kaufen , and y 6 = EOS \mathbf{y}_6=\text{EOS} y 6 ​ = EOS .

To begin with, the encoder processes the complete input sequence X 1 : 7 \mathbf{X}_{1:7} X 1 : 7 ​ = "I want to buy a car" (represented by the light green vectors) to a contextualized encoded sequence X ‾ 1 : 7 \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:7} X 1 : 7 ​ . E.g. x ‾ 4 \mathbf{\overline{x}}_4 x 4 ​ defines an encoding that depends not only on the input x 4 \mathbf{x}_4 x 4 ​ = "buy", but also on all other words "I", "want", "to", "a", "car" and "EOS", i.e. the context.

Next, the input encoding X ‾ 1 : 7 \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:7} X 1 : 7 ​ together with the BOS vector, i.e. y 0 \mathbf{y}_0 y 0 ​ , is fed to the decoder. The decoder processes the inputs X ‾ 1 : 7 \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:7} X 1 : 7 ​ and y 0 \mathbf{y}_0 y 0 ​ to the first logit l 1 \mathbf{l}_1 l 1 ​ (shown in darker red) to define the conditional distribution of the first target vector y 1 \mathbf{y}_1 y 1 ​ :

p θ e n c , d e c ( y ∣ y 0 , X 1 : 7 ) = p θ e n c , d e c ( y ∣ BOS , I want to buy a car EOS ) = p θ d e c ( y ∣ BOS , X ‾ 1 : 7 ) . p_{\theta_{enc, dec}}(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{X}_{1:7}) = p_{\theta_{enc, dec}}(\mathbf{y} | \text{BOS}, \text{I want to buy a car EOS}) = p_{\theta_{dec}}(\mathbf{y} | \text{BOS}, \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:7}). p θ e n c , d ec ​ ​ ( y ∣ y 0 ​ , X 1 : 7 ​ ) = p θ e n c , d ec ​ ​ ( y ∣ BOS , I want to buy a car EOS ) = p θ d ec ​ ​ ( y ∣ BOS , X 1 : 7 ​ ) .

Next, the first target vector y 1 \mathbf{y}_1 y 1 ​ = Ich \text{Ich} Ich is sampled from the distribution (represented by the grey arrows) and can now be fed to the decoder again. And so on in auto-regressive fashion.

It is important to understand that the encoder is only used in the first forward pass to map X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ to X ‾ 1 : n \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ . As of the second forward pass, the decoder can directly make use of the previously calculated encoding X ‾ 1 : n \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ . For clarity, let's illustrate the first and the second forward pass for our example above.

As can be seen, only in step i = 1 i=1 i = 1 do we have to encode "I want to buy a car EOS" to X ‾ 1 : 7 \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:7} X 1 : 7 ​ . At step i = 2 i=2 i = 2 , the contextualized encodings of "I want to buy a car EOS" are simply reused by the decoder.

In 🤗Transformers, this auto-regressive generation is done under-the-hood when calling the .generate() method. Let's use one of our translation models to see this in action.

<pad> Ich will ein Auto kaufen

Calling .generate() does many things under-the-hood. First, it passes the input_ids to the encoder. Second, it passes a pre-defined token, which is the <pad> \text{<pad>} <pad> symbol in the case of MarianMTModel along with the encoded input_ids to the decoder. Third, it applies the beam search decoding mechanism to auto-regressively sample the next output word of the last decoder output 1 {}^1 1 . For more detail on how beam search decoding works, one is advised to read this blog post.

The transformer-based encoder defines a mapping from the input sequence X 1 : n \mathbf{X}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ to a contextualized encoding sequence X ‾ 1 : n \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n} X 1 : n ​ .

The transformer-based decoder defines the conditional distribution p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , X ‾ 1 : n ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , X 1 : n ​ ) .

Given an appropriate decoding mechanism, the output sequence Y 1 : m \mathbf{Y}_{1:m} Y 1 : m ​ can auto-regressively be sampled from p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , X ‾ 1 : n ) , ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , m } p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}), \forall i \in \{1, \ldots, m\} p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , X 1 : n ​ ) , ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , m } .

More specifically, we will see exactly how the encoder makes use of the self-attention layer to yield a sequence of context-dependent vector encodings and how self-attention layers allow for efficient parallelization. Then, we will explain in detail how the self-attention layer works in the decoder model and how the decoder is conditioned on the encoder's output with cross-attention layers to define the conditional distribution p θ dec ( y i ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 , X ‾ 1 : n ) p_{\theta_{\text{dec}}}(\mathbf{y}_i | \mathbf{Y}_{0: i-1}, \mathbf{\overline{X}}_{1:n}) p θ dec ​ ​ ( y i ​ ∣ Y 0 : i − 1 ​ , X 1 : n ​ ) . Along, the way it will become obvious how transformer-based encoder-decoder models solve the long-range dependencies problem of RNN-based encoder-decoder models.
